summary: Some DHCP options carry unique identifiers that can enable tracking even when other identifiers are randomized. This standards-track RFC defines anonymity profiles for clients that want to remain anonymous on a visited network, with guidelines on composing DHCP and DHCPv6 messages to minimize identifying information.

eli5.summary: Walking into a new building without a name tag. This tells devices what to leave out when asking for network settings so they are harder to follow.

questions: what is the dhcp anonymity profile
why randomize mac address and dhcp identifier
subtitle: Guidelines for DHCP and DHCPv6 clients that want to stop leaking identifying details to the networks they visit.

tldr.problem: Several DHCP and DHCPv6 options carry unique identifiers that can be used to track a device even when its link-layer address is randomized.
tldr.mechanism: The anonymity profiles limit which options a client sends, derive identifiers from the current randomized link-layer address, and avoid options and values that reveal past networks or the device's software.
tldr.outcome: A client following the profiles reveals less to the visited network, at the cost of stable addresses and some server features such as name publishing.

facts.label: DHCPv6 DUID to use with randomized MAC

today: RFC 7844 is a Proposed Standard and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Its guidance applies to clients; server privacy is left for further study in the text.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The RFC starts from reports of systems monitoring the wireless connections of passengers at Canadian airports. Privacy-conscious users may respond by randomizing low-level identifiers such as MAC addresses. But as soon as a device connects, it uses DHCP or DHCPv6, and the analysis in RFC 7819 and RFC 7824 shows that their parameters can reveal device identifiers and undo the benefit of address randomization.

Without a common standard, each vendor would minimize disclosure differently, and monitors could use the differences to identify the software on the device. The anonymity profiles provide one shared recipe so that clients look alike.
sections.eli5: If everyone hides their name tag in a different way, the way you hide it can give you away. A shared recipe makes everyone look the same.

sections.title: The Tracking Problem
sections.content:
Wi-Fi sends the MAC address in cleartext in packet headers, even when the payload is encrypted, so anyone listening can see it. Correlating MAC addresses with other data can link devices to owners. The obvious fix is to replace the MAC address with a random 48-bit value before joining a network. Randomization was tried at the IETF meeting in Honolulu in November 2014.

The RFC lists randomization strategies: per connection, per network, and time interval. Changing addresses often is disruptive: the Wi-Fi connection must be re-established, IP addresses change and TCP connections must be restarted. The profiles assume per connection, per network, or an interval about as long as the average connection.

The link-layer address, IP address and DHCP identifier must change in synchrony. If only one changes, an observer can link old and new values. The profiles therefore derive most identifiers from the current link-layer address.

Two limits are acknowledged. Radio fingerprinting of the transmitter's signal cannot be stopped by address randomization and is out of scope. Operating system fingerprinting from option choices and values is something the profiles try to reduce.
sections.eli5: Your device shouts a unique number everywhere it goes. Changing the number helps only if every other label you wear changes at the same time.

sections.title: Design Choices and Limits
sections.content:
The profiles deliberately do not announce that the client wants anonymity. The RFC compares declaring a preference for privacy to wearing a Guy Fawkes mask: it makes you stand out and may trigger extra surveillance. Mitigations should look like ordinary client behavior where possible.

The assumption is that a request for anonymity shows up as a randomized link-layer address. The RFC warns that very frequent changes could exhaust DHCPv4 address pools and increase IPv6 neighbor discovery traffic, so implementers must pick the renewal frequency carefully.

Stable client identifiers give clients consistent parameters, as in RFC 7618, so static clients will normally not use the profiles. Only clients are covered; privacy for DHCP servers is left for further study.
sections.eli5: If you wear a sign saying you want to be invisible, people notice you. It is better to blend in quietly.

sections.title: The DHCPv4 Profile
sections.content:
The profile limits what each DHCPv4 message carries. DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPREQUEST and DHCPINFORM MUST contain the Message Type option, MAY contain Client Identifier and MAY contain Parameter Request List, and SHOULD NOT contain other options (a DHCPREQUEST answering an offer must also carry the Server Identifier and Requested IP address). Clients SHOULD randomize the order of options, or else order them by option code.

  • Client IP address (ciaddr): MUST NOT carry an address obtained with a different link-layer address.
  • Requested IP address (code 50): SHOULD NOT be used in DHCPDISCOVER, but MUST be used where DHCP requires it. In the INIT-REBOOT state a privacy-minded client SHOULD do a full four-way handshake.
  • Client hardware address: use the new randomized value.
  • Client Identifier (code 61): MUST be based solely on the link-layer address in use, contradicting RFC 4361 on purpose.
  • Parameter Request List (code 55): request a minimal number of options and shuffle their order.
  • Host Name (code 12): SHOULD NOT be sent; if sent, MUST be unqualified and obfuscated.
  • Client FQDN (code 81): SHOULD NOT be sent, or MAY use a local-only name.
  • PXE UUID/GUID (code 97): nodes visiting untrusted networks MUST NOT send it.
  • Vendor options (codes 43, 60, 124, 125): SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.eli5: When asking for network settings, only say the few things you must, mix up the order, and never give your real nickname or the maker of your device.

sections.title: The DHCPv6 Profile
sections.content:
When router advertisements allow stateless address configuration, clients SHOULD use it instead of stateful DHCPv6, since it discloses less. Clients SHOULD limit options, and randomize their order as in DHCPv4.

  • Confirm messages: SHOULD NOT be sent, since the addresses in them reveal previous attachment points. A client MAY send one if it can verify the previous and current links are the same network.
  • Client Identifier (code 1): with randomized link-layer addresses, clients MUST use DUID format 3 (link-layer address). Without them, clients SHOULD generate a new random DUID-LLT on each new link, with a randomized link address and a random timestamp from the previous year.
  • Information-request: clients SHOULD NOT include a client identifier.
  • Server Identifier (code 2): MUST only include values received with the current link-layer address.
  • IA_NA (code 3): SHOULD be used; the IAID MUST NOT enable client identification. A suggested IAID is one octet for the interface number plus the first 3 octets of the link-layer address. IA_TA (code 4) SHOULD NOT be used, since it also signals a wish for privacy.
  • Prefix delegation: a client requesting one prefix SHOULD set the IAID to zero and SHOULD NOT include a previously assigned prefix.
  • Option Request (code 6): request a minimal subset and shuffle; SHOULD NOT include previous option values.
  • Authentication (code 11), User Class (15), Vendor Class (16), Client FQDN (39): SHOULD NOT be used, with narrow exceptions such as trusted networks.
sections.eli5: The IPv6 version has the same idea: use a made-up ID that matches your current disguise, skip the extras that point to your old locations, and do not hand over your device's brand.

sections.title: Operational Consequences
sections.content:
The profiles hide the client from the DHCP server, which is not always wanted. Some servers publish names and addresses in the DNS or reassign the same address to returning clients. A client that changes its link-layer address and asks for a new IP address leaves the old one marked as leased, using more resources. Some servers only give addresses to pre-registered MAC addresses, forcing a choice between anonymity and connectivity.

Implementers SHOULD let clients control when the profiles apply, and MAY tie them to link-layer address randomization.
sections.eli5: Hiding your name means the building cannot save your favorite seat or put your name on the door. That is the price of blending in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the use of the anonymity profiles does not change the security considerations of DHCPv4 (RFC 2131) or DHCPv6 (RFC 3315). The privacy trade-offs are covered in the earlier sections.
sections.eli5: Using the profiles does not make the underlying DHCP rules any safer or less safe.

viz.caption: DHCPV4 OPTIONS AND THE PROFILE'S ADVICE

items.label: Host Name
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be sent; if sent, unqualified and obfuscated.

items.label: Requested IP Address
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be in DHCPDISCOVER; MUST be used where DHCP requires.

items.label: Client Identifier
items.desc: MUST be based solely on the current link-layer address.

items.label: Client FQDN
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be sent, or use a local-only name.

items.label: UUID/GUID Client Machine Identifier
items.desc: MUST NOT be sent on untrusted networks.

viz.caption: DHCPV6 OPTIONS AND THE PROFILE'S ADVICE

items.label: Client Identifier
items.desc: DUID format 3 with randomized link-layer address.

items.label: Server Identifier
items.desc: Only values received with the current link-layer address.

items.label: IA_NA
items.desc: SHOULD be used; IAID must not identify the client.

items.label: Option Request
items.desc: Minimal, shuffled; no previous option values.

items.label: Authentication
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be used, except in trusted environments.

items.label: Client FQDN
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be included; a local-only name is allowed.
